scenario:

The subject vehicle is equipped with a standard set of four mounted tyres (two front, two rear) as supplied by the original equipment manufacturer (OEM). Each tyre shall have a unique identification code (e.g., DOT code) visibly marked on the sidewall.

The test facility shall ensure that the vehicle type‑approval documentation package is available, including the vehicle specification sheet, tyre data sheet, and the type‑approval certificate. The documentation shall be reviewed to confirm that the identification codes of all mounted tyres are recorded accurately.

Post‑condition requirements: As required by clause 6.2.3 of UN Regulation No. 152, the mounted tyres shall be identified and recorded in the vehicle type approval documentation.

title: k‑Test method, unladen vehicle at 30 km/h
scenario:
Two vehicles of Category M1 (AA saloon) shall be positioned on a straight, level test track with a dry asphalt surface. The subject vehicle is equipped with the Autonomous Emergency Braking System (AEBS) under test and is unladen; the lead vehicle is a stationary target equipped with a calibrated impact sensor.

The subject vehicle shall accelerate to a steady speed of 30 km/h (tolerance +0/‑2 km/h). Once the speed is stable for at least 2 s, the functional part of the test begins when the distance between the vehicles corresponds to a Time‑to‑Collision (TTC) of 4 s, calculated from the current speed.

Post‑condition requirements: As required by clause 6.1.1.3 of UN Regulation No. 152, the AEBS shall initiate braking such that the vehicle speed is reduced by at least 20 km/h before the calculated collision point, demonstrating compliance with the k‑test method.
preconditions: Subject vehicle: Category M1 AA saloon, unladen, equipped with AEBS and data acquisition system.
Test environment: Straight, level dry asphalt test track, ambient temperature 20 °C ± 5 °C.
test_steps: 1. Position the subject vehicle 40 m behind the stationary lead vehicle and verify alignment on the test track.
2. Accelerate the subject vehicle to 30 km/h (±2 km/h) and maintain this speed for a minimum of 2 s.
3. When the TTC reaches 4 s, activate the AEBS and record the vehicle speed, deceleration profile, and distance to the lead vehicle until the vehicle comes to a stop or passes the collision point.
4. Compare the recorded speed reduction against the required 20 km/h reduction before the collision point.
expected_behavior: The AEBS shall reduce the vehicle speed by at least 20 km/h before reaching the calculated collision point, as stipulated by the k‑test method.
reasoning_trace: Clause 6.1.1.3 references the k‑test method, which defines a test procedure rather than a numeric performance limit. No performance tables are attached, so a single representative test case is generated.

title: AEBS Self‑Check and Immediate Warning Signal after Electrically Detectable Failure
scenario:
Two vehicles of Category M1 AA saloon shall be positioned on a dry, level test track. The subject vehicle is equipped with an Automatic Emergency Braking System (AEBS) and a functional warning‑signal lamp. The vehicle is loaded to its Mass in Running Order (MiRO) and the ambient temperature is maintained between 20 °C and 25 °C.

The vehicle shall be powered on and the AEBS shall be in its normal operational mode. An electrically detectable fault shall be introduced into the AEBS control unit by disconnecting a designated diagnostic line, which the system recognises as a failure condition.

Immediately after the fault is introduced, the AEBS shall perform its periodic self‑check. The self‑check shall be completed and the warning‑signal lamp shall illuminate without an appreciable time interval, defined as no more than 0.5 s between the end of the self‑check and the start of the illumination.
preconditions: Subject vehicle is Category M1 AA saloon, equipped with a calibrated AEBS and warning‑signal lamp.
Test track is dry, level, and conforms to the UNECE test‑track specifications for AEBS functional testing.
test_steps: 1. Power on the vehicle and verify that the AEBS status indicator shows ‘ready’.
2. Introduce an electrically detectable failure by disconnecting the diagnostic line as specified in the test equipment list.
3. Observe the AEBS self‑check sequence and record the time from the start of the self‑check to the activation of the warning‑signal lamp using a high‑resolution data logger.
4. Compare the measured interval with the maximum allowable interval of 0.5 s and document the result.
expected_behavior: The interval between the completion of the AEBS self‑check and the illumination of the warning‑signal lamp shall not exceed 0.5 seconds, satisfying the timing requirement of clause 5.1.4.1.1.
reasoning_trace: The clause specifies a measurable timing requirement for AEBS self‑checks and warning‑signal illumination after an electrically detectable failure, but no performance table is attached. Hence it is a performance requirement and requires a single test case.

title: Verification of Test Surface – Flat, Dry Concrete or Asphalt with Good Adhesion
scenario:
Two vehicles of Category M1 AA saloon shall be positioned on a test track. The test track surface shall be a flat, dry concrete or asphalt pavement that provides good adhesion, as defined by the friction coefficient meeting the minimum value specified in the relevant UN Regulation annexes. The subject vehicle shall be equipped with the system under test (e.g., AEBS) and be in a ready‑to‑test condition. No additional loads shall be applied to the vehicle (unladen condition). title: Driver interrupt of collision warning and emergency braking
scenario:
Two vehicles of Category M1 AA saloon shall be positioned on a dry, level test track. The subject vehicle is equipped with an Automatic Emergency Braking System (AEBS) and a driver‑operated interrupt control (e.g., a dedicated button or switch). The lead vehicle is stationary and positioned 30 m ahead of the subject vehicle. The subject vehicle is unladen and the test is conducted under clear weather conditions.

The subject vehicle shall accelerate to a speed of 50 km/h (tolerance +0/‑2 km/h) and maintain a straight‑line approach toward the stationary lead vehicle. When the AEBS issues a collision warning (audible and visual cue), the driver shall immediately activate the interrupt control to cancel the warning and prevent the emergency braking from being applied. The driver’s action shall occur within 1 s of the warning onset.

Post-condition requirements: As required by clause 5.3.1 of UN Regulation No. 152, the AEBS shall provide the means for the driver to interrupt the collision warning and the emergency braking.
preconditions: Subject vehicle is a Category M1 AA saloon equipped with a functional AEBS and a driver‑operated interrupt control.
Test track is dry, level, and free of obstacles; weather conditions are clear.
test_steps: 1. Position the subject vehicle 30 m behind a stationary lead vehicle on the test track.
2. Accelerate the subject vehicle to 50 km/h (±2 km/h) and maintain a straight‑line approach.
3. Observe the AEBS warning activation; when the warning appears, the driver presses the interrupt control within 1 s.
4. Verify that the AEBS does not initiate emergency braking after the interrupt command.
5. Record the time between warning onset and driver interrupt, and confirm that no braking is applied.
expected_behavior: The AEBS shall cease the collision warning and must not apply emergency braking after the driver activates the interrupt control within 1 s of warning onset.

title: Safety Concept Verification – Single Unit Failure Simulation
scenario:
Two test benches are prepared: one representing the vehicle’s electronic control system (ECS) and the other emulating the vehicle’s mechanical actuators. The subject vehicle is a Category M1 passenger car equipped with the full set of electronic safety functions (e.g., ABS, ESC, AEBS). The vehicle is placed on a static test platform with all wheels locked to prevent motion. All diagnostic connections are made to allow injection of fault signals into individual electronic units.

The test engineer selects a single electronic unit (e.g., the wheel‑speed sensor module) and applies a fault‑simulation signal that mimics a loss‑of‑signal condition. The fault is introduced while the system is powered on and in a ready state. The engineer observes the system’s reaction, focusing on vehicle controllability aspects (e.g., brake command inhibition) and user‑information displays (HMI warnings, indicator lights).

Post-condition requirements: As required by clause 3.9 of UN Regulation No. 152, the safety concept verification test shall demonstrate that the system’s reaction to a single unit failure is documented, that any loss of vehicle controllability is mitigated, and that appropriate user‑information is provided.
preconditions: The test vehicle is a Category M1 passenger car equipped with the complete set of electronic safety functions.
The vehicle is positioned on a static test platform with all wheels immobilised and power supplied to the electronic control system.
test_steps: 1. Connect the fault‑injection interface to the selected electronic unit (e.g., wheel‑speed sensor module).
2. Activate the fault simulation to emulate a loss‑of‑signal condition while the system is in the ready state.
3. Observe and record the system’s response, including any changes to brake command output, vehicle stability control actions, and HMI warnings.
4. Verify that the observed response matches the safety concept requirements and document the results.
expected_behavior: The system shall either maintain safe vehicle controllability (e.g., by applying a safe‑brake strategy) or transition to a safe state, and shall present a clear HMI warning indicating the fault, as stipulated by the safety concept.

title: AEBS manual deactivation requires two deliberate actions
scenario:
Two vehicles of Category M1 (AA saloon) shall be prepared on a dry, level test track. The subject vehicle is equipped with a fully functional Autonomous Emergency Braking System (AEBS) and the driver’s seat is occupied by a qualified test operator. All vehicle systems, including the AEBS, are powered on and the system is in the *active* state.

The test operator shall attempt to deactivate the AEBS using the standard manual deactivation control (e.g., a button or switch) with a single deliberate action – defined as a single press of the control lasting no longer than 0.5 s. The system response shall be observed.

Subsequently, the test operator shall perform two deliberate actions as defined by the regulation: a first press of the deactivation control followed by a second press after a pause of at least 1 s, each press lasting no longer than 0.5 s. The system response shall be observed again.

Post-condition requirements: As required by clause 5.4.1.2 of UN Regulation No. 152, the AEBS shall not deactivate after fewer than two deliberate actions, and shall deactivate only after two deliberate actions have been performed.

Test track surface dry, level, and free of obstacles; ambient temperature 15‑25 °C.
test_steps: 1. Power on the vehicle and verify that the AEBS indicator shows the system is active.
2. Perform a single deliberate action on the manual deactivation control (one press ≤ 0.5 s).
3. Observe and record whether the AEBS indicator changes to the deactivated state.
4. Reset the AEBS to the active state (if necessary) and wait 30 s to ensure system stability.
5. Perform two deliberate actions: press the deactivation control, wait ≥ 1 s, then press again (each press ≤ 0.5 s).
6. Observe and record whether the AEBS indicator changes to the deactivated state.
7. Document all observations and compare them with the expected behaviour.

title: AEBS effectiveness under magnetic and electrical field exposure
scenario:
Two vehicles of Category M1 (AA saloon) shall be positioned on a dry, level test track. The subject vehicle is equipped with a calibrated AEBS and a data‑acquisition system capable of measuring vehicle speed, braking distance and AEBS activation time. A Helmholtz coil system is installed beside the test track to generate a uniform magnetic field, and a parallel‑plate electrode system is installed to generate a uniform electric field across the vehicle path.

The subject vehicle shall accelerate to a steady speed of 50 km/h (tolerance ± 2 km/h) and maintain this speed for at least 5 s before the functional part of the test begins. At the moment the vehicle reaches the predefined trigger point (Time‑to‑Collision ≥ 4 s to a stationary target placed 30 m ahead), the magnetic field shall be set to 0.2 T and the electric field to 5 kV/m. The AEBS shall be activated automatically by the on‑board sensor suite.

Post‑condition requirements: As required by clause 5.1.2 of UN Regulation No. 152, the AEBS shall retain its effectiveness and shall not exhibit any adverse performance degradation when operating under the specified magnetic and electrical fields.
preconditions: Vehicle category M1 AA saloon equipped with a calibrated AEBS and data‑acquisition system.
Test track is dry, level, and free of obstacles; magnetic field generator capable of 0.2 T and electric field generator capable of 5 kV/m are installed and verified.
test_steps: 1. Verify that the magnetic and electric field generators are set to 0 T and 0 kV/m respectively and record baseline AEBS braking performance (stopping distance) at 50 km/h.
2. Increase the magnetic field to 0.2 T and the electric field to 5 kV/m while the vehicle maintains the 50 km/h speed.
3. When the vehicle reaches the trigger point (TTC ≥ 4 s to the stationary target), allow the AEBS to engage automatically and record the braking distance, deceleration profile, and activation time.
4. Compare the measured braking distance under field exposure with the baseline distance and assess compliance.
expected_behavior: The braking distance measured under the 0.2 T magnetic field and 5 kV/m electric field shall not exceed the baseline (no‑field) braking distance by more than 5 % (i.e., Δdistance ≤ 0.05 × baseline), thereby demonstrating that AEBS effectiveness is not adversely affected.

title: Verification of test surface slope within 0 %–1 % range
scenario:
Two test vehicles of Category M1 AA saloon shall be positioned on the designated test track. The test track segment to be used for the AEBS performance test shall be prepared such that its longitudinal slope is uniform across the entire length required for the test.

scenario:

title: AEBS automatic re‑activation after driver‑initiated deactivation
scenario:
Two vehicles of Category M1 AA saloon shall be positioned on a straight, dry asphalt test track. The subject vehicle is equipped with a calibrated AEBS and a data‑logging system capable of reporting the AEBS status (ACTIVE/INACTIVE) in real time.

The driver of the subject vehicle shall initially engage the AEBS by pressing the activation button and verify that the system status reads ACTIVE. The driver then manually deactivates the AEBS by applying the service brake firmly for at least 2 seconds, which according to the regulation triggers an automatic deactivation of the AEBS. After the brake pedal is released and the vehicle speed stabilises below 5 km/h, the condition that caused the automatic deactivation is no longer present.

Post‑condition requirements: As required by clause 5.4.2.2 of UN Regulation No. 152, the AEBS function shall be automatically reactivated as soon as the conditions that led to the automatic deactivation are not present anymore.

2. Apply the service brake firmly for ≥2 s to trigger automatic deactivation of the AEBS; verify the status indicator changes to INACTIVE.
3. Release the brake pedal, bring vehicle speed below 5 km/h, and maintain straight‑line travel for 3 s.
4. Observe the AEBS status indicator; record the time elapsed from brake release to the moment the status returns to ACTIVE.
5. Compare the observed re‑activation time with the requirement that re‑activation occurs immediately once the deactivation condition is removed.
expected_behavior: The AEBS status shall change from INACTIVE to ACTIVE within 0.5 seconds after the brake pedal is released and the vehicle speed is ≤5 km/h, demonstrating immediate re‑activation as stipulated by clause 5.4.2.2.

title: Verification of Road Test Surface Peak Braking Coefficient (PBC) of 0.9
scenario:
Two calibrated measurement devices shall be prepared: a portable deceleration sled and a high‑speed video analysis system, each capable of determining the peak braking coefficient of a road surface. The test shall be conducted on the designated road test surface used for vehicle braking performance evaluations. The surface shall be clean, dry, and free of debris, and ambient temperature shall be maintained between 15 °C and 25 °C. The measurement devices shall be positioned according to the procedures described in UN Regulation No. 152 Annex A.

The first measurement device shall accelerate a test sled to a speed of 30 km/h (tolerance ± 2 km/h) and allow it to brake to a stop on the surface, recording the deceleration curve. The second measurement device shall capture the same event with high‑speed video to independently compute the peak braking coefficient. Both measurements shall be performed consecutively on the same surface segment, and the surface shall not be altered between measurements.

Post-condition requirements: As required by clause 6.1.1.1 of UN Regulation No. 152, the road test surface shall have a nominal peak braking coefficient (PBC) of 0.9 when measured using either of the prescribed methods.
preconditions: The road test surface is clean, dry, and free of debris, with ambient temperature 15 °C–25 °C.
Calibration of the portable deceleration sled and high‑speed video analysis system has been completed according to manufacturer specifications.
test_steps: 1. Position the deceleration sled at the start line of the test surface and set the target speed to 30 km/h (± 2 km/h).
2. Release the sled, allowing it to brake to a stop while the sled records the deceleration curve.
3. Immediately repeat the run while the high‑speed video system records the event for independent PBC calculation.
4. Compute the peak braking coefficient from both data sets and compare each result to the required value of 0.9.
5. Document the measured PBC values, measurement method, and any observed deviations.
expected_behavior: The peak braking coefficient measured by each method shall be equal to or greater than 0.9, within the measurement uncertainty defined in the regulation.

title: Verification of "The System" function on a curved road at 30 km/h
scenario:
Two vehicles of Category M1 AA saloon shall be positioned on a test track that includes a curve with a radius not exceeding 25 m on the outer side of the road. Guard pipes shall be installed on the outer edge of the curve, and a stationary object shall be placed at the curve entry as shown in Figure 3 of the regulation.

The subject vehicle shall be equipped with the fully integrated "The System" and calibrated measurement equipment for speed, time‑to‑collision (TTC) and position. The vehicle shall be unladen and the road surface shall be dry asphalt.

The subject vehicle shall accelerate to a speed of 30 km/h (tolerance +0/‑2 km/h) and travel straight toward the curve. When the vehicle reaches a point where the TTC to the stationary object is 1.6 s, the driver shall initiate the turn into the curve. The vehicle shall decelerate by braking so that its speed at the exact moment it enters the curve is not less than 22 km/h. While traversing the curve, the vehicle shall maintain a constant speed of at least 21 km/h. The TTC to the stationary object shall not exceed 1.1 s when the overlap ratio between the subject vehicle and the stationary object becomes 0 % or when the offset ratio to the centre of the stationary pedestrian/bicycle target reaches –100 %.

Post-condition requirements: As required by clause 3.8 of UN Regulation No. 152, the verification test shall produce a documented result confirming that "The System" operated under the specified non‑fault conditions and satisfied all speed and TTC thresholds defined in the scenario.

2. Monitor TTC to the stationary object; when TTC reaches 1.6 s, initiate the turn into the curve while applying brake to achieve a speed ≥ 22 km/h at curve entry.
3. Maintain a constant speed of ≥ 21 km/h while traversing the curve and ensure TTC does not exceed 1.1 s at the defined overlap/offset conditions.
4. Record all speed, TTC and positional data; verify that the recorded values meet the thresholds and generate the verification result as stipulated.
expected_behavior: The system shall operate without fault, maintaining a speed ≥ 22 km/h at curve entry and ≥ 21 km/h throughout the curve, and TTC shall remain ≤ 1.6 s at turn start and ≤ 1.1 s at the defined overlap/offset points.

title: Vehicle mass condition test per clause 6.2.1
scenario:

The fuel tank shall be filled to at least 50 % of its nominal capacity and may decrease during the series of runs but must never fall below this threshold.

The first test run shall be performed at the mass in running order plus an additional mass not exceeding 125 kg. This additional mass shall include the measuring equipment and the second person, if present. No alteration of the load distribution shall be made once the test procedure has begun.

The second test run shall be performed at the vehicle’s maximum permissible mass, again respecting the same load distribution and fuel‑level constraints.

Post-condition requirements: As required by clause 6.2.1 of UN Regulation No. 152, the vehicle shall have been tested at (a) the mass in running order with a maximum of 125 kg of additional mass and (b) the maximum mass, with load distribution unchanged and fuel level never dropping below 50 % during the series of test runs.

title: AEBS deactivation requires two deliberate driver actions after ESC manual off
scenario:
Two vehicles of Category M1 AA saloon are prepared on a dry, level test track. The subject vehicle is equipped with an Electronic Stability Control (ESC) system and an Autonomous Emergency Braking System (AEBS). The vehicle is loaded to its standard operating mass (unladen) and all tires are inflated to the manufacturer‑specified pressure. The driver is seated in the normal driving position with the steering wheel, accelerator, brake, and ESC off‑switch within easy reach.

The driver first initiates a manual ESC deactivation by pressing the ESC off‑switch and confirming the action on the vehicle’s instrument cluster. Immediately after the ESC is switched off, the driver performs a second deliberate action, such as pressing the AEBS master‑off button or selecting the AEBS off mode via the infotainment menu, to attempt to deactivate the AEBS. The vehicle is stationary during the actions to avoid any unintended vehicle motion.

Post-condition requirements: As required by clause 5.4.2.3 of UN Regulation No. 152, the AEBS shall not deactivate after a single driver action; it shall require at least two deliberate actions by the driver when the ESC function is manually switched off.
preconditions: Subject vehicle is a Category M1 AA saloon equipped with ESC and AEBS, loaded unladen on a dry, level test surface.
Driver has access to the ESC off‑switch and the AEBS deactivation control (master‑off button or menu).
test_steps: 1. Verify that the ESC system is active and the AEBS is enabled prior to the test.
2. Driver presses the ESC off‑switch and confirms the deactivation on the instrument cluster.
3. Driver immediately performs a second deliberate action to deactivate the AEBS (e.g., press AEBS master‑off button).
4. Observe whether the AEBS deactivates after the first action alone or only after the second action.
5. Record the system state (AEBS active/inactive) after each driver action.
expected_behavior: The AEBS shall remain active after the first driver action (ESC off) and shall only deactivate after the second deliberate driver action, satisfying the requirement of at least two deliberate actions.

scenario:

### Overview

Two vehicles are positioned on a flat, horizontal, dry test track under ambient illumination of at least 2000 Lux and temperature above 0 °C. The subject vehicle is a Category N1 light commercial vehicle equipped with an AEBS, loaded to its maximum permissible mass. A pedestrian target crosses perpendicularly at a lateral speed not exceeding 5 km/h, with the anticipated impact point displaced no more than 0.2 m from the vehicle longitudinal centre plane. The road is straight with no curves or intersections.

The subject vehicle accelerates to 25 km/h (tolerance +0/‑2 km/h) and proceeds straight toward the crossing point. When the Time‑to‑Collision (TTC) reaches 4 s, the AEBS shall intervene autonomously. The vehicle continues under AEBS control until the impact point.

Post‑condition requirements: As required by clause 5.2.2.4 of UN Regulation No. 152, the AEBS shall achieve an impact speed less than or equal to 0.00 km/h.

### Preconditions

- Category N1 light commercial vehicle, loaded to maximum mass
- Flat, horizontal, dry road surface; ambient illumination ≥2000 Lux; temperature >0 °C; no adverse weather
- AEBS active, no driver input, system ready for autonomous braking
- Calibrated high‑speed video and lidar system for measuring vehicle speed and impact speed

4. When TTC = 4 s, allow the AEBS to detect the crossing pedestrian and initiate braking; record the vehicle speed profile and impact speed.
5. Compare the measured impact speed with the maximum allowed value (0.00 km/h) and document pass/fail.

- Impact speed shall be ≤ 0.00 km/h.
- AEBS shall activate autonomously without driver input and apply braking to achieve the required impact speed.

Two vehicles are positioned on a flat, horizontal, dry test track under ambient illumination of at least 2000 Lux and temperature above 0 °C. The subject vehicle is a Category N1 light commercial vehicle equipped with an AEBS, loaded to its maximum permissible mass. A pedestrian target crosses perpendicularly at a lateral speed not exceeding 5 km/h, with the anticipated impact point displaced no more than 0.2 m from the vehicle longitudinal centre plane. The road is straight with no curves or intersections.

The subject vehicle accelerates to 50 km/h (tolerance +0/‑2 km/h) and proceeds straight toward the crossing point. When the Time‑to‑Collision (TTC) reaches 4 s, the AEBS shall intervene autonomously. The vehicle continues under AEBS control until the impact point.

### Preconditions

- Category N1 light commercial vehicle, loaded to maximum mass

- AEBS active, no driver input, system ready for autonomous braking
- Calibrated high‑speed video and lidar system for measuring vehicle speed and impact speed

5. Compare the measured impact speed with the maximum allowed value (30.00 km/h) and document pass/fail.
